extracted.intended_audience: newspaper obituary reporters / city reporters / obit desk staff
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, procedural, and stylistic guidance for reporters and editors who gather, prepare, and write newspaper obituaries — including handling photos, building morgue files, verifying deaths, structuring leads and biographies, and appropriate tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling obit photographs
rubrics_metrics.description: Obit pictures must be kept clean and protected; engravers and typesetters have dirty hands, so specific handling steps are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark lightly but largely on the back of the picture "Obit — handle carefully, please don't soil." Retrieve the photo before any inky-fingered apprentice touches it; keep the photo and its frame clean; inspect the press roll to ensure no obit pictures have been transposed (a wrong-person picture is an enormous blunder); return the photo to the family speedily — if in doubt about the office system, the reporter should mail or return the photo personally. Taking back a soiled/torn photo can damage the paper's reputation and prevent future lending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify death reports before publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Under no circumstances does the obit reporter let an unverified death get into the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the voice of each undertaker and verify suspicious calls by telephoning the undertaker with specific questions (e.g., ask about the funeral time) to detect fakery. If there is the slightest hesitation about a supposed call from an undertaker, find out whether that call was genuine. Beware prank or false announcements — they are serious, not funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use undertakers as primary immediate information source
rubrics_metrics.description: Undertakers are the only dependable source of immediate information because doctors and official sources may be slow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train undertakers to call the paper whenever they have 'a case.' In return, give the paper's obituary line credit (e.g., "The Kingsley Company is in charge of funeral arrangements") and furnish undertakers with biographical blanks to fill out. Build cooperative relationships so the undertaker will supply usable information promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain and build the morgue (obit files)
rubrics_metrics.description: The obit column is built upon the files; maintain a large, up-to-date morgue of biographical sketches for prominent residents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rod invests months enlarging the obit files and more time keeping them up to date. If a career is already recorded in the files, the reporter isn't cramped by limited time before edition. Regularly revise entries to bring them up to date; typewrite any longhand material as soon as possible to avoid illegibility later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who belongs in the morgue (nine categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Which residents should be listed in the morgue? The page lists nine groups to include.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include: (1) all present and past members of city government and permanent city officials; (2) all fairly prominent private citizens; (3) professional persons (doctors, lawyers, ministers, educators, architects); (4) prominent business, commercial, and industrial men and women; (5) prominent politicians and labor leaders; (6) those active in lodges, charities, churches, civic work; (7) those in hazardous callings; (8) prominent members of racial/ethnic groups; (9) persons interesting though not important. A good morgue will have hundreds or thousands of career sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gather biographical information tactfully with a blank form
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a blank form with entries for family, lodge, church, political connections, occupations (with dates), honors and achievements to collect obituary material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present the form as building a record for those prominent in the news rather than implying mortality (do not say 'You're almost seventy and might pop off any moment'). Have people fill forms and typewrite longhand responses promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep records legible and regularly revised
rubrics_metrics.description: Typewrite longhand information as soon as possible and periodically revise entries to keep them current.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legible, typed records prevent confusion later; routinely update older entries (example: a biographical blank twelve years old may miss recent important activity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish and keep consistent hospital-contact schedules
rubrics_metrics.description: If hospital-calling is part of the job, call hospitals at specified, consistent hours to gain cooperation and prompt answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep a fixed time (example: 12:15 noon daily) so switchboard operators expect the call and have information ready. Calling at inconsistent times inconveniences busy staff and reduces cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency biographies: prepare and use local knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: When morgue files lack a sketch, go to the house to gather emergency biographical material, but fortify yourself first by consulting friends, associates, and the undertaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult close friends or associates before visiting to obtain a framework; rely on the undertaker to manage distraught relatives and extract information. Be prepared to find family members distraught or unable to help; know the city well enough to find people who can supply authoritative information when language or grief impede answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit tributes sparingly and appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Tributes should not be used too freely; only notables or nearly notables merit (many) tributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain tributes from persons whose comments are worthy — those in high places or those who had particularly good opportunity to know the deceased. Avoid mawkish overuse of tributes for minor persons (e.g., mayor and aldermen weeping for a low-level stenographer). Seek specific, revealing comments rather than gushy lamentation; specific anecdotes (even from low-status witnesses like an elevator operator) can be valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling the 'black sheep' (past misdeeds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to mention past offenses (prison, disbarment, etc.) based on the deceased's public status and relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the person was a public character or held public office, mention significant past misconduct. For entirely private citizens who only attracted attention because of a single misstep — especially if they've lived it down — the likely answer is 'No.' Use the guiding principle of obituary writing: make the story friendly, sympathetic, and dignified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obituary tone: natural, friendly, dignified; avoid saccharin and color writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The style should be one of natural, friendly dignity, free from saccharine phrases, light or humorous treatment, and overwriting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sentimental language such as 'he leaves a wife and six children to mourn the tragedy of his untimely passing.' Avoid attempts to make readers weep; overwriting typically produces maudlin copy that editors will cut. The reporter should aim for calmness and reasonableness in presenting difficult facts (example provided in the page).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid judging newsworthiness by wealth, retirement, or politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume a retired person is of little news interest; do not equate importance with bank account; do not let political affiliation affect obituary completeness or warmth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three things never to do: (1) assume retirement diminishes news interest — older readers may value a once-prominent name; (2) judge a person's newsworthiness by his bank account — modest means can still hide importance; (3) allow politics to affect the obituary — party affiliation does not justify belittling a person's life. Avoid partisan comments or belittling political failures in obits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use facts rather than adjectives to show prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer specific factual statements (a 'factual adjective') to vague laudatory adjectives like 'prominent' or 'respected.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specific, concrete identification (e.g., 'for n years the captain in command of No. 2 fire station') is more powerful than 'prominent officer in the fire department.' Facts convey prominence without relying on overused adjectives; over-adjectiving dulls impact and can appear inconsistent if applied to some but not all subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve interpretation and evaluation for suitable cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretive obituaries (passing judgment) are generally reserved for public personages or when the facts alone do not tell the whole story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public figures (e.g., an ex-mayor) or those with accomplishments that warrant evaluation may receive interpretive obits. Ensure evaluations are supported by concrete accomplishments (e.g., listing municipal achievements to justify an assessment). For nonpublic persons who were inventors or notable in specialized ways, provide appropriate interpretation if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know religious funeral practices and report accurately
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand and correctly report religious funeral forms and terminology; small mistakes annoy readers of faith communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the practices (example: Roman Catholic Requiem High Mass scheduling and personnel). Use complete phrasing preferred by the community, name priests who officiate, deacons and subdeacons, and if priests sit in the sanctuary, name them. An ordinary priest may sing while a monsignor acts as subdeacon — report these details correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: News identification in the lead: identify the person to attract readers
rubrics_metrics.description: The main burden of the obit lead is to identify the person so readers know at once whether they wish to read about his career; pick the one or two identifications that will attract the most reader interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid weak leads that only give age and address. Use identifiers such as profession plus a known location or notable offices held (example progression: address → 'prominent druggist' → 'proprietor of the Memorial Square drugstore' → add length of establishment and board membership). When a person has several claims to attention, use a long lead highlighting the best one or two items, with other aspects summarized in a second paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate lead length and angle (short vs long vs long lead with multiple IDs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select short or long leads depending on how many claims to attention the subject has and which identifications will best attract readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If several interest angles exist, use a long lead that presents multiple identifications (store proprietor, community chest director, photography club founder, lodge master) so various readers find a personal link. If one aspect dominates, a focused lead is appropriate. Consider which identifications will evoke personal familiarity or impress broad readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give the obituary a single unifying theme for coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: An obituary must emphasize a single theme or impression to give the reader something to remember the person by; without coherence the obit is a failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify a unifying thread (example: 'a man of perpetual activity') that relates disparate career elements and illuminates the subject's life. Avoid shoveling dispersive, disorganized information at the reader; present material that supports the chosen theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure the obituary in blocks (lead, genealogy, funeral arrangements, biographical sketch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the obituary's elements in blocks rather than scattering them throughout the piece to aid readability and coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four elements: (i) the lead with news identifications and circumstances of death; (ii) genealogy/list of relatives; (iii) funeral arrangements; (iv) the biographical sketch. Keep each element together rather than diffusing family history across the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose among four practical block arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange blocks in four different designs depending on the subject and the length of the biography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design 1: lead → genealogy → funeral plans → biographical sketch (effective for very well-known subjects). Design 2: lead → biographical sketch → funeral plans → relatives (good when biography must come early to show readers the subject's importance). Design 3: lead → highlights of biography → relatives → funeral plans → details of biography (useful when many readers will be satisfied with highlights). Design 4: lead → condensed biography → detailed biography → relatives → genealogy (good for subjects with many activities; keeps condensed sketch near details).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use two-part (divided) biographies when long
rubrics_metrics.description: If the biography is long, split it into a condensed/highlight sketch and a more detailed presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This device (adopted from wire services) furnishes high spots early for casual readers and places details lower for interested readers. Two-part biographies can be arranged within the four block structures to balance immediate identification and detailed information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biographical sketch organization: chronological or reverse chronology
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange biographical material logically, either from birth forward (chronological) or from recent career backward (reversed chronology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the order that best serves coherence and the unifying theme: e.g., Chronological (Born 1895 → Educated at → Main career ...) or Reversed Chronology (Recent career → Main career → Born ...).
